evaluation.positioning_hook: A timid office clerk in a retro-futurist death bureau is forced into a monster hunt when his buried anomaly powers make him the team’s last chance to erase a regenerating British zombie.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The hook is instantly legible — dead-end office worker, secret power, monster mission — and the comedy-action blend gives it a clear genre audience. It’s still a narrower buy than a four-quadrant fantasy because the humor is very specific and the world is eccentric rather than broadly accessible.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands fast in the opening pages: Francis wakes in the logistics division of Comirum, gets conscripted, and is told he’s a SINON with erased-outburst powers. The mission objective is clear by the London street sequence, and the script keeps the central question simple: what can Francis actually do?

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Francis has a strong underdog engine — anxious, resistant, funny, and secretly powerful — and Ploy, Clara, Hal, and Toast all pop as distinct team colors. The limitation is that most of the supporting cast is built as vivid comic function more than deep contradiction, so the role appeal is strongest for the lead and a few scene-stealers.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s bureaucratic afterlife/monster-response setting has a fresh visual and comic identity, especially the death-toll board, the outburst monitor, and the absurdly specific team dynamics. The British-zombie target and the multilingual, retro-futurist office texture give it a confident weirdness that feels authored.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script moves efficiently from office disruption to team assembly to London confrontation, and the action escalates cleanly once the zombie appears. The middle stretch is more setup-and-banters than pressure-cooker escalation, so the propulsion is solid rather than relentless.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea — a powerless-seeming clerk whose anomaly can erase threats — is easy to grasp and commercially ownable, while still feeling unusual in execution. It’s fresh enough to stand out, but the underlying structure is still a familiar reluctant-hero monster mission.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Comirum feels like a functioning institution with rules, ranks, and internal slang, and the logistics division, briefing room, cafeteria, and mission transport all suggest a larger machine beyond the page. The world is story-generating because every character seems to have a job, a power, and a place in the hierarchy.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is sharply pitched as deadpan workplace absurdism colliding with grotesque action, and the script commits to that register consistently. The comic-sans death board, the donut/chocolate bit, and the team’s casual cruelty all lock in a distinct voice.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Francis’ opening flash of the empty college ruins and the color-shifted eyes hints at a larger mystery around his powers and identity. That depth is present but still mostly implied; the page is more interested in immediate comic momentum than in layering a deeper emotional mythology.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The team chemistry is the main engine here: Francis/Ploy, Francis/Hal, Doreen/Hal, Clara/Toast all generate distinct friction and banter. It’s not a fully elastic ensemble yet, but there’s enough interplay that multiple pairings can carry scenes.

lead_characters.name: Francis Booker
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 20s to early 30s, office worker, anomalous supernatural ability, likely working-class/underclass-coded
lead_characters.hook: Francis is a terrified logistics clerk who wants nothing more than to stay invisible, do spreadsheets, and avoid the field — but he’s also the one person in Comirum whose outbursts can apparently erase reality. He reads as a reluctant, self-protective underdog with a comic mouth and a buried power he doesn’t understand, and the script keeps him funny even when he’s panicking.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jesse Eisenberg in The Social Network or Steven Yeun in Beef — a tightly wound, fast-talking lead who gets to play fear, irritation, and sudden authority in the same scene. The role gives an actor a clean transformation arc and a late-movie power reveal that can reframe the whole performance.

lead_characters.name: Ploy
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 20s-30s, Thai, field operative with sonic/bass-based powers
lead_characters.hook: Ploy is the loud, teasing, high-energy operator who immediately clocks Francis as a fellow outsider and pushes him toward action. She’s flirtatious, reckless, and emotionally direct, with enough swagger to feel like she’s always one beat ahead of the room.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Janelle Monáe in Glass Onion or Auliʻi Cravalho in The Little Mermaid a chance to dominate scenes through charisma and rhythm. It offers a performer a big personality part with action utility and comic timing.

lead_characters.name: Doreen
lead_characters.hook: Doreen is the hard-edged boss who treats apocalypse logistics like a personnel problem and never wastes a word she doesn’t need. She’s controlled, intimidating, and pragmatic, but the script lets flashes of dry humor leak through her armor.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong Glenn Close in The Wife or Viola Davis in Fences energy — a command-performance role where authority, restraint, and buried feeling do the work. It gives an actor the pleasure of being the room’s gravitational center without needing speeches to announce it.

lead_characters.name: Hal
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s-40s, physically imposing, field operative with enhanced strength
lead_characters.hook: Hal is the swaggering bruiser who jokes about WWII and seems to enjoy being underestimated almost as much as he enjoys violence. He’s a loud, macho team presence, but the script also frames him as someone who can take a hit and keep the room moving.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do the Bautista-in-Guardians of the Galaxy thing — deadpan physicality with comic self-awareness. It’s a showcase for size, timing, and the ability to make a blunt instrument feel lovable.

lead_characters.name: Clara
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 20s-30s, Italian, coked-up, volatile field operative
lead_characters.hook: Clara is a feral, hypersexual, drug-fueled chaos agent who talks like she’s always mid-party and mid-fight at the same time. She’s dangerous, funny, and unpredictable, with a live-wire energy that makes every entrance feel like a disruption.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the same scene-stealing volatility as Jennifer Coolidge in The White Lotus or Anya Taylor-Joy in The Menu, but with more physical action. It’s a big swing part built on rhythm, attitude, and comic menace.

lead_characters.name: Toast
lead_characters.demographics: Nonhuman robot, adult-coded, sentient machine operative
lead_characters.hook: Toast is the dry, contemptuous robot who treats everyone else like inferior biology and says the quiet part out loud. The character is all precision, sarcasm, and tactical competence, which makes him a perfect straight-man counterweight to the chaos around him.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of voice-and-presence role that lets an actor do what Alan Tudyk does in Rogue One or what Paul Bettany does as Vision — precision delivery, comic disdain, and a distinct nonhuman rhythm. It’s a performance showcase even when the face is less expressive than the voice.

lead_characters.name: Jerry
lead_characters.demographics: Male, adult, cyborg wolf-man, office worker
lead_characters.hook: Jerry is the hungry, friendly, physically odd office presence who turns a simple donut gag into a world-building beat. He’s not central to the mission, but he helps sell Comirum as a place where the weird is normalized.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a fun character-actor slot in the vein of Doug Jones-style creature work or a scene-stealing supporting turn in a creature comedy. It gives an actor a memorable physicality and a single strong comic beat.

casting_characteristics: one lead with strong comedic panic and late-film power reveal
ensemble of highly stylized supporting roles
nonhuman and creature-adjacent casting for Toast and Jerry
multilingual dialogue and accent-specific performance for Ploy and Clara

notable_requirements: office floor with cubicles and chalkboard

technical.vfx_details: multicolor energy bursts, body-erasure effects, wrist-device UI, teleportation/light transport, zombie regeneration, glitch effects, and a robot character likely requiring enhancement or full CG integration
technical.sfx_needs: practical weapon effects, blood, limb loss, regeneration gags, impact hits, and creature makeup/prosthetics for the zombie and cyborg wolf-man

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model; best positioned as a streamer-friendly genre title with limited theatrical upside

budget.note: The contemporary office material is cheap, but the London night exteriors, creature/zombie work, teleportation effects, and multicolor erasure climax will keep this above a simple contained indie.

casting.note: Francis needs an actor who can play anxious comedy and late-film power release, while Clara, Hal, Ploy, and Toast all need very specific tonal precision to avoid flattening the ensemble.

development.note: The script’s appeal is tied to its oddball world and team chemistry, so the buyer conversation will focus on whether the Comirum mythology and Francis’ anomaly are enough to sustain a feature-length arc.

comp_set.title: The Suicide Squad
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the irreverent team-of-misfits energy, violent comic-book absurdity, and a mission structure where the ensemble chemistry is the main selling point.

comp_set.title: Deadpool
comp_set.why_it_comps: Comps on the self-aware, profanity-forward comic tone and the way a reluctant antihero becomes the audience’s guide through escalating chaos.

comp_set.title: Men in Black
comp_set.why_it_comps: The bureaucratic secret-agency framework, monster-of-the-week energy, and deadpan institutional worldbuilding are the closest mainstream analog.

comp_set.title: The Mitchells vs. the Machines
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the offbeat family-of-outsiders dynamic and the visual inventiveness around a misfit lead discovering unexpected competence.

audience_target.primary_audience: Genre fans who like irreverent action-comedy with a weird workplace-world and a reluctant underdog lead.
audience_target.demographics: 18-44 skew, slightly male-leaning but with strong crossover for viewers who respond to ensemble banter and stylized genre comedy.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary interiors keep the base manageable, but the creature work, VFX climax, night exteriors, and stylized action push it above microbudget territory.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane of smart, weird, effects-light-to-moderate genre features that sell on voice, ensemble chemistry, and a clean hook. The office-bureaucracy setting and comic violence make it especially friendly to buyers looking for a distinctive but producible genre swing.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature: the world is fun, but the page does not yet define a separate spin-off vector with enough depth to justify franchise planning.

strengths.what_it_means: This gives the project a clean, marketable identity that can be pitched in one breath and understood instantly by buyers. It’s the kind of premise that attracts streamer genre execs and indie financiers looking for a fresh container rather than a generic monster movie.
strengths.evidence: The death-toll board, logistics division, outburst monitor, and cubicle setting all establish a bizarre workplace with rules before the mission even starts.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Francis is a strong reluctant-lead role.
strengths.what_it_means: The lead part has real casting value because it starts as comic impotence and ends with a power reveal, which is exactly the kind of arc that can reframe an actor’s range. That makes the script attractive to managers packaging a breakout or a mid-career reset.
strengths.evidence: Francis repeatedly insists he can’t do the mission, then discovers the hot dog triggers his anomaly and erases the zombie with a multicolor beam.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ensemble has distinct comic textures.
strengths.what_it_means: Each supporting character brings a different performance lane — swagger, menace, deadpan, chaos, flirtation — which creates multiple casting hooks and scene-stealing opportunities. That broadens the project’s appeal to actors and gives the film more than one memorable face.
strengths.evidence: Ploy’s bass weapon, Clara’s drugged volatility, Hal’s macho bravado, and Toast’s contemptuous precision all play differently.

strengths.what_it_means: A buyer can see the lane immediately: irreverent, violent, and weird without losing the emotional spine of an underdog story. That specificity helps the script stand out in a crowded genre market where many projects blur together.
strengths.evidence: Comic-sans death board, donut banter, profanity, and grotesque zombie action all coexist without the script losing its voice.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The world feels expandable and lived-in.
strengths.what_it_means: Comirum reads like a place with internal systems, which is valuable because it makes the movie feel bigger than the scenes on the page. Buyers often respond to worlds that imply more story than they explicitly show, especially in genre.
strengths.evidence: The logistics division, mission briefing, cafeteria, hallway politics, and article-based termination language all suggest a functioning institution.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, pitchable genre feature with a memorable workplace hook, a breakout-ready lead role, and an ensemble that can sell on character as much as spectacle. It lives in a buyer-friendly lane: contained enough to finance, weird enough to stand out, and commercial enough to give a streamer or indie financier a real packaging conversation.

items.area: The hot-dog trigger is the whole mechanism.
items.detail: Francis’ breakthrough depends on a very specific gag — eating the alley hot dog to unlock the anomaly — which is memorable but also makes the climax feel contingent on a single comic beat. That’s the sharpest buyer question in the script because the emotional payoff is tied to a mechanism that reads as arbitrary until the reveal lands.

items.area: The supporting team is more color than depth.
items.detail: Ploy, Clara, Hal, and Toast are all vivid, but the page mostly uses them as tonal functions around Francis rather than giving them independent emotional engines. That’s fine for a contained feature, but it limits the ensemble’s long-tail value and narrows the project’s appeal to actors looking for meatier secondary arcs.

The London street sequence leans on regeneration, glitching, teleportation, multicolor erasure, and creature damage to land the finale. It’s manageable at this scale, but buyers will immediately factor in whether the visual payoff can be delivered cleanly without the movie feeling underpowered.

items.area: The world is specific but still mostly surface-level.
items.detail: Comirum has strong texture, but the script only hints at the larger rules of SINONs, the outburst system, and the agency’s hierarchy. That gives the movie style and mystery, but it also means the deeper mythology is still a promise rather than a fully bankable asset.

issues.headline: The script’s main friction is that its biggest payoff depends on a very particular comic mechanism, and the supporting ensemble is still functioning more as flavor than as fully dimensional counterweights. Add in a finale that needs clean VFX execution, and the buyer conversation becomes less about concept and more about whether the movie can land its weirdness at feature scale.
